intuition: All the words have the same length, so read the string in whole-word chunks. Keep a moving group of chunks and count each word. Remove chunks from the left if a word appears too often. Try each possible starting alignment so no valid starting position is missed.

There are width possible alignments, one for each starting offset modulo word length. Within one alignment, keep word occurrence counts and a count of tokens currently held. An unknown word invalidates every window crossing it, so clear the state. A known word that exceeds its required count requires removing tokens from the left until that required count is respected again.

At this point every retained count is at most its required count. If the total number of retained tokens equals the number of required words, all required counts must be exact. This establishes a match without comparing complete dictionaries. Scanning every alignment also finds starts that are not multiples of the word width, and retaining the window permits overlapping matches.
If the entire concatenation is longer than s, no starting index can fit it. The reference returns immediately before allocating frequency maps or scanning alignments in that case.

steps: For s="barfoothefoobarman" and words=["foo","bar"], width=3 and both required counts are one.
At offset 0, read "bar", then "foo". The valid window has two tokens, so record left=0.
The next token "the" is unknown. Clear counts and set left to the index after it, 9.
Read "foo" at index 9 and "bar" at 12; the two required counts are satisfied again, so record 9.
The final "man" resets the window. Other alignments contribute no matches, leaving [0,9].

concept.question: Can equal word lengths turn a letter scan into a moving bag of words?
intuition: Trying every start and recounting all its words repeats work. Equal word lengths give fixed-size chunks, but a valid start might be aligned at any letter position within one chunk width.

For each possible alignment, move a frame in whole-word chunks. Maintain how many copies of each required word it contains. Unknown chunks empty the frame; too many copies of a known word move the start forward until its count is allowed.
concept.observation: The frame must contain exactly the required number of copies of every word, not merely the right distinct words.
approach: Try each alignment within one word width.
Extend by a whole chunk, resetting on unknown words and shrinking excessive counts.
Record a start when the frame contains the full required word collection.
concept.correctness: Within one alignment, the frame contains only allowed chunks with counts no greater than required. Once its chunk count equals the required total, these bounded counts must all match exactly. Excess-count shrinking preserves all later valid starts, and reset discards only frames containing an impossible chunk. The alignment passes together examine all starts.

complexity.explanation: Each alignment advances forward in chunks. Including chunk slicing and counting, work is proportional to the text length times the word width. Remember counts for distinct words and the current framed collection.

pitfalls: Check every alignment within a word width.
Shrink when a word is overrepresented, rather than discarding all potentially useful chunks.
